column2: The South's system of racial slavery, which bound white and black southerners together and shaped the region's identity.
The expanding Lower South cotton belt, stretching into the Mississippi valley and Texas, that fueled the southern economy and drove the slave population steadily westward and southward.
The claim that cotton dominated the southern economy and, by extension, American prosperity, because the United States came to produce most of the world's cotton.
The older slave states that shifted toward wheat and corn, required less labor for those new crops, and sold surplus slaves to planters in the Deep South.
The newer plantation region of cotton, rice, and sugar, including the Black Belt and the Mississippi valley, where slavery was most heavily concentrated.
The fertile plantation region of central Alabama and Mississippi that became a major destination of the westward cotton boom.
The forced sale of enslaved men, women, and children from the Upper South to planters in the Deep South, which separated many husbands from wives and children from parents.
The small elite defined by ownership of 20 or more slaves.
A large staple-crop operation managed as a complex business by the master.
The nonslaveowning white majority, most of them landowning, semisubsistence farmers who raised primarily corn and hogs on modest farms with family labor.
The small bottom layer of white southern society, poverty-stricken and disdained by other whites as "crackers," "white trash," "sand-hillers," or "clay-eaters."
The ideal that the master provided care and guidance of dependent "children," including the people he enslaved.
The older, more refined plantation society of the Chesapeake and the South Carolina coast, which modeled itself on the English country gentleman and built Greek Revival mansions.

The newer society of the cotton kingdom, still at or just emerging from the frontier stage, where many planters were self-made men who used aggressive business tactics and often lived in simple unpainted frame houses.
A labor system, predominant in the cotton districts, in which a white overseer or a Black driver supervised groups of about 20 to 25 adults for long hours of closely watched work.
A labor system, most common in the rice fields, in which each slave received a specific daily assignment and was finished for the day once it was done, working at his or her own pace.
Sexual relations between whites and Blacks, especially the relationships between white men and enslaved women that plantation mistresses condemned but could not prevent.
Religious songs that slaves sang at work, at play, and in worship, often with a hidden element of protest beneath seemingly meek, otherworldly language.
Slave stories, often with animal characters such as the cunning Brer Rabbit, that laughed at the master's shortcomings and taught the young how to survive in a hostile world.
Secret woods or quarter gatherings where slaves met at night to worship beyond the master's control, with rhythmic singing and dancing modeled on the ring shout.
The proslavery claim, associated with John C. Calhoun, that slavery was not a necessary evil but a benefit.
The congressional rule, demanded by southern leaders, that blocked consideration of antislavery petitions.
